data.title: Hana Chorvátová: Lunula pendants and their meaning
data.excerpt: Following her introduction to pendants and amulets, the historian and archaeologist Hana Chorvátová turns to lunulae – crescent-shaped pendants that appear in only a handful of graves in the early medieval cemeteries of the Carpathian Basin. She traces their lunar symbolism from Greek and Roman mythology to Christian art and asks why they were placed above all in the graves of small girls.

children.text: Following the introductory article by the historian and archaeologist Hana Chorvátová on pendants and amulets in general, we continue today with an equally interesting discussion of lunulae in the Early Middle Ages and their interpretation.

Lunula pendants attract attention because they occur only in very small numbers in early medieval cemeteries in the Carpathian Basin. At cemeteries where the number of graves ran into considerable figures, they were usually found in only one, or at most five, graves.
From the 9th–11th centuries, for example from Staré Město, where 1,492 graves were found, a lunula had been placed in the grave of only three individuals.
A lunula was found in five graves at the cemetery at Dolní Věstonice, where more than a thousand graves are known.
An exception is the cemetery at Majs (c. 1,200 graves), where a lunula appeared in 18 graves.
From the period of the Avar Khaganate, graves are known that yielded several lunulae each. At Üllő there were nine pieces in a single grave,
three pieces each were found in graves at the cemeteries at Holiare,
Nové Zámky
and Želovce.
In the 9th to 11th centuries only a single lunula occurs in a grave. The exception is again the cemetery at Majs (graves nos. 53, 681, 806, 1031 and 1126), where two lunulae also occurred in graves.
A higher number has not so far been recorded.

Of all the finds of lunula pendants so far known from the Carpathian Basin, in only 120 cases is it certain that the lunulae come from a grave assemblage (finds of lunulae from the Migration Period were excluded from the analysis). Within this group the age of the individuals is not determined in 38 cases (31.6%). Of the remaining 82 burials, 57 (69.5%) were children and adolescents and 25 (30.4%) were adult women. These figures show that children's graves considerably outnumber the graves of adult women. Even where a lunula was found with a child's skeleton, these remains of a child can be attributed to the female sex on the basis of the other accompanying material (the exceptions are two graves from the cemetery at Staré Město (47/51 and 132/51), in which boys were buried).

An analysis of jewellery (earrings, necklaces with pendants) in relation to the age and sex of the deceased, carried out on Great Moravian cemeteries, showed that jewellery is associated above all with the graves of small (infans I) and young girls.
In the later period (the 11th–12th centuries) too, jewellery appears above all in the graves of girl children.

On the basis of these facts it may be supposed that the placing of a lunula in graves, especially those of children, had a particular meaning, which, however, remains hidden from us. One can attempt only a slight unveiling of the symbol of the lunula.

The shape and the name of the pendant leave us in no doubt that the form of the pendant was derived from the crescent moon, and we may assume with high probability that the pendant is connected with the Moon, as many authors suppose.

M. Eliade, who studied the history of religions and the religious ideas of various historical civilisations, sought to bring closer and to clarify for present-day people the various ideas and phenomena that the people of ancient civilisations associated with the Moon. In his view it was lunar symbolism that made it possible to bring into relation and mutual affinity such diverse facts as: birth, death, resurrection; water, the plant, woman, fertility, immortality, cosmic darkness, prenatal life and the consecrated existence followed by a rebirth of the lunar type; weaving, the symbol of the ´thread of Life´, fate, temporality, death, and so on.“

Thanks to the moon and its phases, that is, its „birth“, „death“ and „resurrection“, man became aware that Death is inseparably bound up with Life and, above all, that Death is not an end but a temporary change followed by a new birth.

Death and fertility are phenomena governed by the Moon. Ethnological observations show that most peoples do not think of death without at the same time thinking of procreation and the propagation of the human race.

The relationship between fertility and the Moon is sometimes obscured by the agrarian deities that appeared with the spread of agriculture, such as the great Mother goddesses and various other gods of fertility (Baal, Ishtar). One characteristic of the Moon always remains the same, although many religions approach it by inventing new „forms“ – and that is: the eternity of fertility, recurring origination and inexhaustible life.

Some animals become symbols of the Moon or even „depict“ it, because their shape or behaviour recalls its properties. The greatest number of properties similar to those of the Moon can be seen in the snake. Because the snake appears and disappears, it is regarded as „the husband of all women“; it sheds its skin, in which a periodic rebirth – immortality – can be seen. The symbolism of the snake is somewhat misleading, but everything points to the central idea of the symbol of the Moon, which is able to perish and come into being again and again and which has a power capable of ensuring fertility, foresight (prophecies) and even immortality. Superstitions are known from the European area which likewise imply a relationship between woman and the Moon – the snake, in connection with the power of the Moon to confer exceptional abilities. One Breton legend records that the hair of witches turned into snakes. There is a certain amount of ethnological evidence that witchcraft is conferred by the Moon, either directly or through snakes. Snakes as „lunar“ animals – that is, eternal – living beneath the earth also embody the souls of the dead, know all secrets, can foretell the future and are a source of wisdom. Thus whoever eats a snake will understand the speech of animals. This cannot be regarded as a symbol with a metaphysical meaning – entry into the transcendental world. This assumption was accepted by ancient scholars as well.

children.text: Of the lunar symbolism, the connection between the Moon and fertility comes to the fore most of all, but so too does the connection of the Moon and of woman – the mother – with virginity, which (at first sight) appears contradictory. Examples of this connection can be found in Greek and Roman mythology, but also in other parts of the world very distant from the Mediterranean, such as the Indonesian archipelago or the territory of the Mexican Indians. Christianity, too, took over the connection of the virgin – the mother – the Moon in a certain way.

Fertility. In the Old Testament it is recorded that the Lord, through the prophet Isaiah, forbids women to wear „crescents for the neck“, which women regarded as an amulet of fertility (Isaiah 13, 8). From the world of the Mexican Indians the connection between the Moon and a woman expecting a child is known. Men help their pregnant wives by praying to the Moon throughout the whole of their pregnancy.
Lunula pendants from the European area are therefore often interpreted as a symbol of fertility.

children.text: The Moon – the mother – the virgin. In the beginnings of Greek mythology, the connection of the Moon, the mother and the virgin was represented by three goddesses who were very closely bound to one another: the Moon – Hecate, the mother – Demeter, the virgin – Persephone. Behind these goddesses there appears the original idea of a connection between three aspects of the world – the virgin, the mother and the Moon.

In the goddess Artemis the Moon – the mother – the virgin are already united in a single being. This goddess is above all a huntress and a protectress of wild animals, and a virgin. Yet many elements of a mother goddess can also be found in her. In Arcadia, at her oldest cult place, she was associated with Demeter and with her daughter Persephone. In some areas she was venerated as a goddess of childbirth. She is assumed to be of Oriental origin.
In a later period the cult of Artemis was identified with the cult of the Moon goddess Selene, and Artemis was venerated as a Moon goddess as well.

A similar development is recorded in Roman mythology too, where the connection of the virgin, the mother and the Moon is found. The goddesses Diana and Juno were above all protectresses of women in childbirth. Later the Moon goddess Luna was identified with them.
From the Indonesian archipelago comes the story of the moon maiden Rabie, in which the connection between the virgin and the Moon appears once again.

children.text: The connection of the moon, the mother and the virgin probably found an echo in Christianity as well. Christian artists very often depicted the Virgin Mary standing or sitting on a crescent moon. They certainly found their inspiration in the Revelation of St John, which speaks of a woman clothed with the sun, with the Moon beneath her feet, who is preparing to give birth.

This perhaps confirms M. Eliade's idea that Christianity certainly brought with it profound and radical modifications in the religious evaluation of the Cosmos and of Life, but did not reject them entirely.

The connection of the Moon and the virgin in ancient mythology, and the fact that lunula pendants appeared in the graves of young girls at the cemetery at Chernihiv, inspired the Russian archaeologist B. A. Rybakov to interpret the lunula as a symbol that denoted girls who were coming of age, or which, in a bride's attire, was to signify that the bride had not yet severed her ties with the group of unmarried girls.

The interpretation of the lunula as a symbol for maturing maidens and brides cannot be accepted. It would presuppose a higher number of these pendants at individual cemeteries. It may therefore be supposed that the pendants were connected with a different symbol.

Lunula pendants were popular and widespread in the Roman period as well. This is attested not only by their occurrence in children's graves, but also by their depiction on busts of children and of women. In that period they were regarded as amulets to which was attributed a power supporting and protecting growth, or a power that was to protect the wearer's health.
Alternatively, the lunulae were seen as a protective amulet guarding against adverse and evil forces.

This meaning of the lunula as a protective amulet in the Late Roman period was perhaps preserved for lunulae of the later period as well. This is probably connected once again with one of the characteristics of the Moon, namely the inexhaustibility of life.

The connection of the lunula with the Moon allows us to consider one further meaning of it. As has already been said, the Moon is also credited with the ability to confer exceptional abilities and to ensure knowledge. The Moon goddesses Selene and Hecate are at the same time regarded as goddesses of spells and magic.

Women – wise women – witches connected with the Moon are known from the European area. The Moon goddesses, as has already been said, are also at the same time protectresses of women in childbirth. Childbirth, then, also stands under the influence of the Moon. M. Eliade states that women's associations (Weiberbünde) are always connected with the mystery of birth and fertility. The mystery of childbirth, that is, of the woman discovering that she is creative at the level of life, represents a religious experience that cannot be rendered in the language of male experience. It is therefore understandable that childbirth became the stimulus for secret female rituals, which many times developed into true mysteries. Traces of such mysteries have survived even in Europe.

children.text: Women – wise women – witches are known in the Slavic world. L. Niederle states that the whole of human life was bound up with these witches. Everything depended on them – a happy birth, health or sickness, fortune or misfortune, a long life or death.

These facts and the rarity of the occurrence of lunula pendants allow us to consider a further meaning of the lunula – namely, that lunulae denoted women – wise women – witches initiated into the mystery of childbirth. But how is it to be explained that we know the pendants above all from the graves of small girls?
Among the Slavs a belief in an afterlife is generally assumed.

From some religions we know of small children being predestined for later consecration (for example in the Lamaist religion) or even for a secular function (for example spurs in the graves of small boys). Perhaps these small girls too were predestined for later initiation into the female mysteries, and the lunula was to make this known to people in the next world. Among scholars concerned with the interpretation of the lunula in the Slavic cultural milieu the view has also been expressed that it is evidence of a lunar cult in which the Moon was venerated as the younger brother of the Sun, or as the bridegroom of the Sun, and exceptionally as a female being.

All the meanings of the lunula mentioned above – ensuring fertility and growth, protection against evil forces, the marking of young girls – virgins, a symbol for wise women – witches – can only be surmised and pondered. Some meanings are more, others less probable. With a high degree of probability, however, the lunula can be connected with woman as such. Evidence of this is provided by a casting mould of the Roman period on which, beside the mould for a pendant in the shape of a phallus – the symbol of man – a mould for a lunula is placed.

The article was originally published in the journal Praehistorica. (K významu lunicových príveskov z včasnostredovekých pohrebísk strednej Európy [On the meaning of lunula pendants from early medieval cemeteries of Central Europe]. In: Praehistorica XXIII. Praha 1998, 135-140.)
